title: Age-inclusive work: distinguishing chronological age from occupation, context, and opportunity
question: Are age differences in work engagement explained by job age-typing and experienced age discrimination rather than chronological age?

documents.text:
# Age-inclusive work: distinguishing chronological age from occupation, context, and opportunity

Narrative review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

How do organizational studies distinguish age-related experiences from stereotypes and institutional constraints?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)).

## Evidence base and method

The author's folder (`Paper 8 Oct 2024/References`) holds 23 PDFs. All were identified against Crossref, and none is retracted. Nine were excluded as off-topic because they concern the aged-care *sector* or population economics rather than workers' age (`screening.json`). The 14 included records are:

- 7 empirical studies: 5 cross-sectional surveys, 1 two-wave survey and 1 multi-study scale development with survey data.
- 7 non-survey pieces: reviews, theoretical frameworks, commentaries and one analysis of collective agreements.

Each was coded for how it handles the three things the question separates:

- **CHRON**: chronological age as a variable
- **STEREO**: stereotypes, ageism or discrimination
- **INST**: institutional or regulatory constraints, such as collective agreements and retirement law
- **PRACT**: organizational age practices
- **JOB**: occupational age-typing

Design and sample details were copied verbatim from each Method section (`extraction.json`). Quotes used below were checked against the cited PDF pages.

## What the collection shows

### 1. Empirical studies mostly test chronological age as a moderator, and often find nothing

In the empirical studies, chronological age is usually a moderator of other relationships.

- A Turkish remote-work study concluded that "the main and interactive associations between age, gender and potential caregiving responsibilities were overall null" [R1, PDF p10]. It backed that conclusion with Bayes factors favouring the null for all non-significant interactions [R1, PDF p10]. This is unusually careful evidence *for* absence.
- A two-wave study found that "the two-way interaction between autonomy and age to predict engagement is non-significant" [R2, PDF p7]. Age mattered only jointly with task variety, in a three-way pattern.
- A study of workers aged 45 and over used age as an eligibility threshold rather than a variable. Its finding concerns mental demands and work ability, not age itself [R3, PDF p14].

The common move is to treat age as a number that may condition other effects. That says little about *why* age would matter: through experience, through stereotypes or through constraints.

### 2. Stereotypes are mostly theorized, rarely measured

Three conceptual pieces put stereotypes at the centre:

- An early review concluded that stereotypes of age-related decline in performance persist, although the physical and cognitive changes of ageing are modifiable [R4, abstract].
- A multilevel framework links cultural values to age discrimination at societal, organizational and individual levels, and offers research propositions [R5, abstract].
- A commentary argued that "Culture broadly writ, as a characteristic of countries or societies, has not been evidenced to affect age stereotypes" [R6, PDF p2]. It cites work in which objective and subjective age interact in how raters stereotype [R6, PDF p2].

Only one empirical study measures discrimination directly. It developed a job age-type spectrum: some jobs are seen as "young" and others as "old". Its discussion reports that "workers whose ages were mismatched to their jobs reported experiencing more age and sex discrimination—but only when these workers were women" [R7, PDF p17]. The same paper reports that the three-way interaction of chronological age, job age-type and sex was not significant in one model [R7, PDF p12]. The intersectional result should be read as specific to particular outcomes and analyses.

This study comes closest to the question. It separates chronological age (the person) from age-typing (the job) and from discrimination (the treatment).

### 3. Institutional constraints are documented, not modelled with individual outcomes

Institutional constraints appear in three ways, none linked to individual outcomes:

- One study analyses Canadian nursing collective agreements for practices that could sustain an ageing workforce, a document-level analysis of provisions [R8, abstract].
- An introductory piece frames ageing-workforce issues through workforce-management policy [R9].
- A conceptual model treats organizational practices for older workers as both shaped by and shaping society and organizations [R10, abstract].

No included empirical study measures an institutional constraint, such as retirement rules, contract terms or pension incentives, alongside workers' experiences.

### 4. Organizational practices are the main empirical bridge

The best-developed empirical line studies age-diversity practices:

- Practices predicted retirement preferences through work engagement, with the direct effect becoming non-significant ("full mediation") [R11, PDF p8].
- In 802 Portuguese workers aged 18–72, practices related to turnover intention through engagement and commitment [R12, PDF p10, p14].
- Among 484 older employees and their leaders, well-being was lower when leaders rated age-friendly practices higher than the employees did. Practices as *perceived* by the affected group, not as declared by the organization, carried the effect [R13, abstract]. Not all congruence hypotheses held: "Hypothesis 1 was thus not supported" [R13, PDF p8].

These studies show how practice and policy reach individuals. All are survey-based, and most are cross-sectional and self-reported.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **The three explanations are rarely separated empirically.** Most studies enter chronological age as a moderator. When age effects appear, nothing in the design says whether they reflect experience, stereotype or constraint.
2. **Null age effects are common and sometimes well-evidenced** [R1, R2]. Age itself may matter less than the age-typing of the job or the treatment people receive.
3. **The most useful design move separates person, job and treatment**: chronological age, job age-type and experienced discrimination [R7]. Institutional constraints have not yet been brought into individual-level designs in this collection.
4. Organizational age practices, measured from both employee and leader perspectives [R13], are the best-supported route from institutions to experience.

## Limits

- 23 PDFs in one curated folder, 14 included, half conceptual. The empirical base is small and mostly cross-sectional.
- No included study is longitudinal over years, so age, cohort and period cannot be separated.
- Full-text extraction relied on machine-copied Method passages plus the quotes above. Some sample details, such as country for some studies, are in `extraction.json` only where the passages stated them.

## Proposed research direction

The companion protocol proposes a design that measures the three explanations separately in the same people: chronological and subjective age; perceived age-typing of one's job and experienced age discrimination; and documented institutional constraints from contracts and HR policy, coded independently. The design is multi-wave, with HR-record outcomes where access permits. It remains a proposal pending population, access and ethics decisions.

# Paper 8 — Empirical protocol v2: Age-inclusive work: separating chronological age, job age-typing and treatment

> **Status: PROPOSAL awaiting AMET University Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval.** No data have been collected; no results exist. Sample sizes are computed from **assumed** smallest effects of interest, not from any study. Instruments are ScaleScope catalogue entries whose source articles were resolved on Crossref (9 October 2026). Version 2 replaces the v1 draft `paper-8-oct-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Research question
Are age differences in work engagement explained by job age-typing and experienced age discrimination rather than chronological age?

## 2. Hypotheses (to be pre-registered)
- H1: Experienced age discrimination predicts lower engagement beyond chronological age.
- H2: Mismatch between age and the job age-type predicts experienced discrimination.
- H3: Documented organisational age practices moderate H1.

## 3. Design
Two-wave survey linked to independently coded organisational policy documents.

**Measurement occasions**
- T1: age, subjective age, job age-type, discrimination
- T2 (3 months): engagement

## 4. Population, eligibility and recruitment
**Population(s):** AMET University faculty and administrative staff; working professionals in India (organisations reached through alumni, professional networks and recruiter contacts); a paid online research panel (Indian working adults).

**Eligibility:** Employed adults (18+); oversample workers aged 45+. Exclusion: failing two or more embedded attention checks; incomplete primary measures at the analysed wave (handled under §8).

**Recruitment and independence safeguards**
- **AMET faculty and staff** — invitation sent by the study team through an institution-wide mailing list with Registrar permission, **not through line managers or HoDs**; nothing is reported at a level smaller than 5 respondents; no participation data reach appraisers.
- **Working professionals in India** — via alumni networks, professional associations and LinkedIn posts; where organisational data (HR records, supervisor ratings) are needed, a signed **organisational access letter / data-sharing agreement** is obtained first and the organisation never sees individual responses.
- **Paid online panel** — a commercial panel provider (to be selected; must allow India-resident adult workers, pre-screening on eligibility, attention checks and payment at or above the provider's fair-pay guidance). Prescreen answers are re-asked inside the survey for verification.

## 5. Measures
| Construct | Instrument (ScaleScope id) | Items | Occasion | Source article (Crossref-verified) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Work engagement | Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES-9, #2) | 9 | T2 | [10.1177/0013164405282471](https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164405282471) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Experienced age discrimination | Workplace Age Discrimination Scale (WADS) (outside catalogue) | see source | T1 | [10.1007/s10869-015-9425-6](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-015-9425-6) | confirm permission/licence; measure confirmed in title/abstract |
| Job age-typing | Job age-type measure (Cleveland & Hollmann items, as validated by Reeves et al.) (outside catalogue) | 2 | T1; two 9-point items rating the respondent’s own job (younger- vs older-worker job); spectrum values from the source as a cross-check | [10.1016/j.jvb.2021.103616](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvb.2021.103616) | confirm permission/licence; measure and items confirmed in full text |
| Subjective age | Subjective age: comparative + felt age (outside catalogue) | 2 | T1; comparative-age item + felt-age-in-years item, wording as in the source | [10.3758/bf03193996](https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193996) | confirm permission/licence; measure and items confirmed in full text |
| Organisational age practices | Age-inclusive HR practices (outside catalogue) | see source | age-inclusive HR practices (source construct) + independent policy-document coding by two coders | [10.1111/peps.12047](https://doi.org/10.1111/peps.12047) | confirm permission/licence; measure confirmed in title/abstract |

All instruments are administered in English (the working language of the target population). Any translation or wording adaptation (e.g. day-level or target-shifted versions) is labelled **adapted — not validated**, piloted with cognitive interviews (n ≈ 10) and checked for factor structure before the main study.

## 6. Sample size
Noncentral-F test of 1 predictor(s) within 6: f² = 0.02 needs **395** completers (80% power, α = .05). With assumed attrition/exclusion of 25% across waves, recruit **527**. *Assumption:* Discrimination effect beyond age and covariates, f² = .02.

Target completers: **395**; recruitment target: **527**. Power will be re-checked by simulation with pilot variances before pre-registration; if the target is not reachable, the study is reported as estimation (confidence intervals) rather than as a confirmatory test.

## 7. Procedure and timing
1. IEC approval → OSF pre-registration (hypotheses, analysis, exclusions, stopping rule) → pilot (n ≈ 30, not analysed for hypotheses).
2. Recruitment window ≈ 6 weeks per wave; two reminders per wave; reminders stop on withdrawal.
3. Waves linked by a self-generated pseudonymous code; the linking key is stored separately from responses.
4. Data collection ends when the recruitment target is met or the pre-registered end date passes, whichever is first.

## 8. Analysis plan
Hierarchical regression / SEM; age-group invariance of measures; moderation by coded practices.

- **Missing data:** full-information maximum likelihood (or multiple imputation, 20+ imputations) under MAR; attrition analysed against baseline variables and reported.
- **Measurement:** CFA for each multi-item measure; reliability (ω and α) reported; measurement invariance across waves/groups before comparing means or paths.
- **Inference:** two-sided α = .05; effect sizes with 95% CIs; Holm correction across the confirmatory hypothesis family; exploratory analyses labelled as such.
- **Common-method bias:** temporal separation and, where planned, other-source ratings; a marker variable is included in the survey.

## 9. Ethics (ICMR 2017 National Ethical Guidelines)
- **Risk category:** Minimal risk — request **expedited review**. Rationale: Questions about everyday work experiences; no deception, no intervention, no identifiable data published.
- **Consent:** written/electronic informed consent before any question; separate consent items for each optional element (record linkage, co-worker/supervisor contact, follow-up waves).
- **Voluntariness:** no penalty for non-participation or withdrawal; no data from or to supervisors/appraisers at individual level.
- **Confidentiality & data protection:** pseudonymised data, linking key held only by the PI on an encrypted drive; processing consistent with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; retention 5 years after publication (or as the IEC directs), then deletion.
- **Support:** debrief page with the national tele-mental-health helpline (Tele-MANAS, 14416 — verify before use) and contact details of the PI and IEC.
- Ethics pack (IEC application summary, participant information sheet, consent form, debrief): `../ethics/paper-8-oct-2024-ethics-pack.md`.

## 10. Open science
OSF pre-registration before data collection; de-identified data and analysis code shared on OSF after publication where consent permits (HR-record and organisational data excluded unless the organisation agrees).

## 11. Approvals and readiness checklist
- [ ] Instrument items obtained

- [ ] Panel provider selected and costed (if panel used)
- [ ] Pilot completed and power re-checked

## B. Participant information sheet
**Study:** Age-inclusive work: separating chronological age, job age-typing and treatment

**Why are we doing this study?** Our research question is: Are age differences in work engagement explained by job age-typing and experienced age discrimination rather than chronological age?

**What will I be asked to do?** Complete online questionnaires (about 15–20 minutes per survey) on 2 occasion(s) as described: T1: age, subjective age, job age-type, discrimination; T2 (3 months): engagement.

**Do I have to take part?** No. Taking part is voluntary. You can stop at any time and withdraw your answers up to the point the data are anonymised for analysis [date], without giving a reason and without any effect on your job, appraisal or relationship with your organisation.

**Risks:** We do not expect any risk beyond everyday life. You can skip any question.

**Benefits:** No direct benefit; a summary of findings will be offered.

**Confidentiality:** Your answers are linked across surveys by a code you create, not by your name. Your supervisor or organisation will never see your individual answers. Results are reported only for groups of 5 or more.
